cards.front: An observational human scan can establish {{c1::association}}, but it does not by itself identify a cause.
cards.quote: An observational human scan can establish association, and careful validation can establish prediction, but neither alone identifies a cause.

cards.front: Why does a matched control strengthen a causal circuit claim without proving it beyond doubt?
cards.back: It holds matched factors constant, reducing alternative explanations, but cannot guarantee that every alternative has been eliminated.
cards.quote: A matched control reduces alternative explanations; it does not make them impossible.

cards.front: A manipulation changes activity only in a named projection during one test window and changes one behavioural assay. How broad may the causal conclusion be?
cards.back: Conclude only that the named projection's activity affects that behaviour in that window and assay. The identifying contrast does not support broader claims about other cells, times, or behaviours.
cards.quote: Every causal circuit claim is only as specific as its identifying contrast

cards.front: Gain of function tests {{c1::sufficiency}}, whereas loss of function tests necessity.
cards.quote: With gain of function already tied to sufficiency and loss of function to necessity, the useful next case is a partial result.
cards.section: From a manipulation to a claim

cards.front: Why can a lesion provide evidence about necessity yet still leave the interpretation complicated?
cards.back: A lesion asks what is lost after damage, but lesion extent, effects on connected networks, and compensation can blur what caused the loss.
cards.quote: lesion extent, connected networks and compensation complicate the answer.
cards.section: From a manipulation to a claim

cards.front: Silencing a neuronal population reduces a behaviour but does not abolish it. What happens to the necessity claim, and why?
cards.back: It is not established. The population contributes under the tested conditions, but necessity requires showing that the specified behaviour cannot occur without its activity in that design.
cards.quote: Silencing a population reduces a behaviour but does not abolish it. Has the experiment shown that the population is necessary?
cards.section: From a manipulation to a claim

cards.front: Which four features should a usable causal circuit claim name?
cards.back: The cells, the projection, the timing, and the measured behaviour.
cards.quote: A usable claim therefore names four things: the cells, the projection, the timing and the measured behaviour.
cards.section: From a manipulation to a claim

cards.front: Artificial activation of a neuronal population produces a behaviour. Does that show the population is the animal's normal or only route to that behaviour?
cards.back: No. Sufficiency under the tested conditions neither establishes that the cells are the only route nor that artificial activation reproduces the unmanipulated animal's normal route.
cards.quote: It does not say that the manipulated cells are the only route to the behaviour
cards.section: From a manipulation to a claim

cards.front: In a construct-by-light design, interaction = {{c1::(opsin light − opsin no light) − (fluorophore light − fluorophore no light)}}.
cards.quote: interaction = (opsin light − opsin no light) − (fluorophore light − fluorophore no light)
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: What does the fluorophore group's light-on minus light-off difference estimate in a two-by-two optogenetic design?
cards.back: It estimates the effect of matched illumination without an opsin.
cards.quote: The second difference estimates what the matched light does without an opsin.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: Wild-type mice with no opsin: continuous striatal illumination at powers used in experiments suppresses firing, and one-sided light biases turning toward the lit side. What does this demonstrate?
cards.back: Illumination itself can change physiology and behaviour in opsin-free tissue, so light-on versus light-off alone cannot identify an opsin effect.
cards.quote: Continuous striatal illumination at powers used in experiments suppressed firing, and one-sided illumination biased turning toward the lit side.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: Opsin-expressing animals change behaviour with light, but the experiment has no illuminated fluorophore-only group. What alternative remains?
cards.back: The light itself may have changed behaviour. A matched opsin-negative light condition is needed to estimate that effect.
cards.quote: They showed that light-on versus light-off, by itself, does not identify an opsin effect.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: Why does illuminating a terminal field not by itself prove that transmission at the named synapse caused a behaviour?
cards.back: Light can excite axons of passage, labelled crossing axons, or activity traveling back toward parent cell bodies.
cards.quote: But illumination in a terminal field is not yet proof that local transmission at the named synapse caused the behaviour.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: Activating basolateral-amygdala cell bodies reduces open-arm time, while activating their terminals in the central amygdala increases it. How must the claim change?
cards.back: Separate region-level activation from projection-specific activation. Cell-body stimulation recruits several outputs together, whereas terminal stimulation names one output.
cards.quote: The terminal experiment names one output, so the claim must distinguish region-level activation from that projection-specific manipulation.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: Activating basolateral-amygdala terminals in the central amygdala reduces anxiety-related behaviour; a local glutamate-receptor block makes that reduction disappear. What does the block test?
cards.back: It tests whether local transmitter action in the terminal field is required for the light-induced behavioural effect.
cards.quote: Tye and colleagues therefore blocked glutamate receptors locally in the central amygdala. The light-induced reduction disappeared.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: Design the minimal construct-by-light experiment that separates an opsin-linked behavioural effect from an effect of illumination itself.
cards.back: Test opsin and fluorophore-only animals with light on and off. Compute the light effect in each construct group, then compare those two effects as the interaction.
cards.quote: The film built a construct-by-light design: opsin or fluorophore only, each tested with light on and off.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: Why should physiology be recorded during and after illumination when validating an optogenetic protocol?
cards.back: To show that the chosen protocol produced the intended physiological change and to detect effects that persist or emerge after light ends.
cards.quote: Record during and after illumination to show that the chosen protocol produced the intended physiological change.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: An optogenetic protocol uses 5 millisecond pulses at 20 hertz. How long is the light on per second, and what is the duty cycle?
cards.back: 20 pulses × 5 ms = 100 ms on per second; 100/1,000 = 0.10, so the duty cycle is 10 percent.
cards.quote: Its stimulation used 5 millisecond pulses at 20 hertz.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: A behavioural effect appears only when light overlaps the task epoch, but the design lacks an off-window condition. What uncertainty remains?
cards.back: The experiment has not isolated timing. Add illumination outside the hypothesized window to test whether the task-linked timing is what matters.
cards.quote: If timing matters, add an off-window condition.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: A light manipulation changes avoidance, but it may also slow movement. What added comparison makes the behavioural interpretation more specific?
cards.back: Add a locomotor control. The rule is to match or measure plausible alternatives so the contrast isolates the claimed behaviour rather than movement generally.
cards.quote: If movement could explain the result, add a locomotor control.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: Which procedural checks reduce bias in allocation, condition order, exclusions, and behavioural scoring?
cards.back: Randomize allocation, counterbalance repeated-condition order, define exclusions in advance, and score behaviour blind.
cards.quote: Randomize allocation, counterbalance repeated-condition order, define exclusions in advance and score behaviour blind.
cards.section: Read the two-by-two as two differences

cards.front: The standardized mean difference is the group difference divided by the {{c1::pooled standard deviation}}.
cards.quote: The standardized mean difference is the group difference divided by that pooled spread
cards.section: Effect size, power and the experimental unit

cards.front: Why is the experimental unit not automatically the number of trials in a behavioural study?
cards.back: Repeated trials can share expression, placement, and state within one animal, so they are nested rather than independent units.
cards.quote: repeated observations share expression, placement and state within an animal.
cards.section: Effect size, power and the experimental unit

cards.front: For two independent groups at 80 percent power and two-sided alpha 0.05, {{c1::n per group = 2 (1.96 + 0.84)^2 / d^2}}.
cards.section: Effect size, power and the experimental unit

cards.front: Two groups have means of 60 s and 48 s with a pooled standard deviation of 12 s. What is the standardized mean difference?
cards.section: Effect size, power and the experimental unit

cards.front: Using n per group = 2(1.96 + 0.84)^2/d^2, what sample does d = 1.0 imply?
cards.back: n = 2(2.80)^2/1.0^2 = 15.68, so round up to 16 animals per group; the lesson notes about 17 with a t distribution.
cards.quote: At d = 1.0, this gives 15.7, so the pilot implies 16 animals per group
cards.section: Effect size, power and the experimental unit

cards.front: A confirmatory study should plan for the {{c1::smallest effect worth detecting}}, not automatically reuse a pilot's effect estimate.
cards.quote: Plan for the smallest effect worth detecting.
cards.section: Effect size, power and the experimental unit

cards.front: Using the same two-group approximation, how many animals per group are needed for d = 0.5?
cards.back: n = 2(2.80)^2/0.5^2 = 15.68/0.25 = 62.72, so round up to 63 animals per group.
cards.quote: the same approximation gives 15.7 divided by 0.25, or 62.7: 63 animals per group.
cards.section: Effect size, power and the experimental unit

cards.front: Eight mice each complete 40 trials, and all 320 trials are analyzed as independent observations. What happens to uncertainty, and why?
cards.back: Uncertainty becomes too small because trials within each animal share variation. Preserve the nesting and identify the independent experimental unit.
cards.quote: Treating them as independent hides that shared variation and makes uncertainty too small
cards.section: Effect size, power and the experimental unit

cards.front: The conventional imaging signal indexes {{c1::blood-oxygenation changes associated with neural activity}}, not spikes.
cards.quote: The conventional imaging signal indexes blood-oxygenation changes associated with neural activity, not spikes.
cards.section: Association, prediction and causation in human imaging

cards.front: In monkey visual cortex, simultaneous electrical and imaging recordings found that local field potentials estimated the imaging signal better than multi-unit activity did. What interpretation did the authors suggest?
cards.back: The signal may reflect input and intracortical processing better than spiking output.
cards.quote: Local field potentials estimated it better than multi-unit activity did
cards.section: Association, prediction and causation in human imaging

cards.front: In the rigorously denoised analysis of 3,928 participants, the median absolute univariate brain-wide association with behaviour was {{c1::0.01}}.
cards.quote: the median absolute univariate brain-wide association with behaviour was 0.01.
cards.section: Association, prediction and causation in human imaging

cards.front: How can a task-fMRI study show clear group-average activation yet still yield a weak individual biomarker?
cards.back: The average response can be clear while individuals' relative rankings are too unstable across repeated measurements for useful prediction.
cards.quote: A group-average activation can be clear while individual rankings are too unstable for a useful biomarker.
cards.section: Association, prediction and causation in human imaging

cards.front: Why do large-sample findings about brain-wide individual differences not set a minimum sample for every imaging design?
cards.back: Their scope is brain-wide individual-difference studies; within-subject designs use each person as their own comparison and answer a different question.
cards.quote: They do not say imaging is broken or set a minimum sample for every within-subject design
cards.section: Association, prediction and causation in human imaging

cards.front: For a true correlation of 0.10 at 80 percent power and two-sided alpha 0.05, use n = (2.80/atanh r)^2 + 3. What approximate sample size is required?
cards.back: atanh(0.10) ≈ 0.1003, so n ≈ (2.80/0.1003)^2 + 3 ≈ 780 using the lesson's rounded calculation.
cards.section: Association, prediction and causation in human imaging

cards.front: In 25 people, an observed correlation is 0.10. Using Fisher z, SE = 1/√(n−3), what is the approximate 95 percent correlation interval?
cards.quote: Converting back gives correlations from about −0.31 to +0.48. The sign is unknown.
cards.section: Association, prediction and causation in human imaging

cards.front: A model selects imaging features using all participants, then cross-validates only model fitting. What happens to the performance estimate, and why?
cards.back: It becomes optimistic, because test-fold outcomes already influenced feature selection. Repeat selection and tuning within each training fold.
cards.quote: The test-fold outcomes already influenced feature selection, so the reported performance is optimistic.
cards.section: Association, prediction and causation in human imaging

cards.front: A model predicts outcomes in genuinely unseen people. What causal conclusion follows from that success?
cards.back: None by itself. Held-out prediction can establish generalization to new people, but the cause of the predicted outcome remains unknown.
cards.quote: A validated predictor may generalize to new people while still leaving the cause of the predicted outcome unknown.
cards.section: Association, prediction and causation in human imaging

cards.front: A disorder-linked study leaks each person's scans across folds, uses only opsin light-on versus light-off, scores behaviour unblinded, and treats trials as replicates. Give one coherent repair strategy.
cards.back: Split human data by person and tune only within training folds. In mice, add the opsin-negative arm, blind scoring, verify physiology, and analyze trials nested within animals. Keep human association separate from mouse causation.
cards.quote: Start by separating three claims: an association in humans, a prediction target and a causal intervention in mice.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: The 2005 cultured-neuron demonstration established reliable {{c1::millisecond-timescale control of spiking}} with channelrhodopsin-2.
cards.quote: showed reliable millisecond-timescale control of spiking.
cards.section: What the first channelrhodopsin experiments established

cards.front: What did the cultured-neuron channelrhodopsin demonstration establish, and what did it not establish?
cards.back: It established control of spikes in chosen cultured cells. It did not establish an intact-animal or behavioural effect.
cards.quote: The neurons came from newborn rats; there was no intact animal and no behaviour.
cards.section: What the first channelrhodopsin experiments established

cards.front: Long channelrhodopsin-driven depolarization can suppress spikes through {{c1::depolarization block}}.
cards.quote: Long channelrhodopsin-driven depolarization can suppress spikes through depolarization block
cards.section: When the construct name misleads

cards.front: A stronger, longer channelrhodopsin stimulus produces fewer spikes than a weaker stimulus. What lesson-stated failure mode could explain this?
cards.back: Depolarization block: prolonged drive can suppress spikes, so harder optical drive can silence the cell meant to be activated.
cards.quote: driving harder can silence the cell meant to be driven.
cards.section: When the construct name misleads

cards.front: Why must the post-light window be included when validating an optogenetic silencing protocol?
cards.back: Abruptly ending silencing can trigger rebound firing, so an effect after light offset belongs in the physiological result.
cards.quote: Abruptly ending silencing can produce rebound firing, so the post-light window belongs in the result.
cards.section: When the construct name misleads
